awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Development of Commercially Viable Cell Lines for Cultivated Fish via Bioengineering
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is a novel means of producing seafood products. The method provides an alternative meat production to wild-caught fisheries of which 90% are at or exceed capacity, with many premium species lacking viable aquaculture models. This novel method of cellular seafood agriculture produces fish meat by growing only the required product such as muscle and fat, using scalable energy sources (e.g. glucose made from corn). The process involves expanding cells in a bioreactor and differentiation, followed by assembly, to produce seafood with no mercury, antibiotics, or microplastics. The initiative aims to supplement domestic seafood production representing one the most widely eaten animal proteins in the world accounting for 17% of all animal protein consumption, while reducing America’s reliance on imports across the $28B domestic seafood market of which 70-85% is imported. 
 
This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to develop cellular agriculture  in a scalable manner to meet cost and quality requirements. The proposed activities will improve the growth rate (cells per time) and maximum density (cells per volume) of specific cell lines in bioreactors. The overall goal is to promote the rapid and efficient proliferation of muscle-forming fish cell lines in suspension culture. This will be accomplished through (Objective 1) transcriptomics and pathway enrichment analysis to identify key genetic targets, (Objective 2), food-safe bioengineering techniques to confirm and modify the expression of these targets and finally (Objective 3) demonstrate efficacy in a pilot production system. This aims to achieve faster growth and higher density than current approaches (allowing desirable traits to spontaneously arise), to greatly improve the unit economics of cellular agriculture. The results from this project will serve as the foundation for future larger efforts to engineer cell lines optimizing growth rate, taste and preparation characteristics at cost and scale for cultivated fish.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Most animal cells grow only when attached to a solid surface. Producers therefore grow them in flat flasks, which limits scalability and keeps costs high. Cells that grow suspended in liquid can be produced in large tanks instead, but few cell types do this naturally. Cells can be slowly forced to adapt to suspension, but they usually stop doing the job they were grown for: liver cells stop processing drugs the way a liver would, and skin cells stop making the collagen they are harvested for.

With support from the National Science Foundation’s Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program, Atlantic Fish Co. investigated whether ordinary surface-dependent cells could be converted to grow in suspension while still doing their original job, initially for cultivated seafood production. The company is now focused on using the technology to support cell production for research and development.

Project activities and key findings. The team measured gene activity in fish muscle cells just after they were moved into suspension. Candidate targets from those measurements were tested with small molecules, and the most effective targets were then disabled permanently using gene editing. The same method was applied to three kinds of primary human cells from donors.

Blocking two signaling systems let cells keep growing in suspension. The edited fish muscle cells grew continuously for more than a month and kept their ability to form muscle. Human skin, bone marrow, and liver cells also grew in suspension using this technology, with early evidence that they kept their original function. One limit emerged along the way. Permanently blocking the two systems pushed cells toward growth and away from making secreted proteins, which matters when the product is the protein rather than the cells themselves. Applying the change temporarily rather than permanently restored normal production, and confirming this over a full production run is ongoing.

Intellectual merit. The project explained why detached cells stop growing, and showed that the same mechanism holds across species and cell types. The editing method needs no added marker gene to identify successfully edited cells, because only edited cells grow in suspension.

Commercial application. This technology offers customers two kinds of value. The first is scale: cells that grow in suspension can be produced in tanks, far more cheaply and in far less space than in flasks. The second is function: the cells that come out still do what the customer needs them to do. Either one alone is of limited use. The current commercial target is the companies that supply primary human cells and the companies that use those cells to make products, in preclinical drug testing, for biomanufacturing, and in laboratory systems that replace animal testing. All of them are limited by how many cells they can produce, because the cells they work with must be grown on surfaces and come from human donors.

Broader impacts. In scenarios modeled with customers, the method cut production cost by roughly 85 percent and the space required by roughly 80 percent. Cheaper cells support domestic manufacturing, laboratory systems that are replacing animal testing, and seafood grown from cells rather than caught. Interviews with dozens of companies redirected the business from cultivated seafood toward supplying human cells, and several are now paying customers.

Next steps. Atlantic Fish Co. has filed for patent protection. The company will extend the method to additional cell types customers have asked for and will test each against quality benchmarks set with those customers. It will also continue to develop the temporary version of the treatment.
